case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s presented to our immunobullous disease clinic with a 30-year history of an intensely pruritic eruption predominantly affecting her legs, forearms, and hands. She also reported a nearly lifelong tendency for skin sloughing with minimal trauma but denied mucosal or nail involvement. Previous treatments, including topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and oral antihistamines, had been ineffective. Her family history was unknown. Results of prior biopsies at an outside institution showed perivascular and focal lichenoid lymphohistiocytic inflammation with milia and a subepidermal separation, suggesting possible epidermolysis bullosa acquisita vs artifactual separation. Physical examination was notable for hundreds of brown to violaceous scaly, lichenoid papules on the anterior lower legs, dorsal feet (Figure, A) and dorsal forearms, some with a linear configuration, with a few scattered lesions on the upper and lower back. Her great toenails and 2 others were dystrophic, but all other nails appeared normal. No blisters were present, and the remaining examination results were otherwise unremarkable. A biopsy for direct immunofluorescence was taken; a repeat biopsy for hematoxylin-eosin staining was performed; and serum was obtained for collagen type 7 antibody assay and genetic testing to rule out epidermolysis bullosa.
case_info.caption: A, Hundreds of reddish-brown 2- to 5-mm flat-topped papules are scattered on the patient’s bilateral lower extremities and dorsal feet with great toenail dystrophy. B, Histopathological imaging shows basketweave hyperkeratosis overlying areas of acanthosis and epidermal thinning and sparse lymphohistiocytic perivascular dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: Repeat hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed sparse perivascular to focally lichenoid dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis without vacuolar change or eosinophilic infiltration (Figure, B). Areas of acanthosis, orthohyperkeratosis, and epidermal thinning were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed no linear deposition of immunoreactants at the basement membrane zone, and the result of the type 7 collagen enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay was negative. Genetic testing identified heterozygosity in theCOL7A1gene for a sequence variant,c.7247G>T, confirming the diagnosis of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). In the setting of lichenified papules on the patient’s extremities, severe refractory pruritus, skin fragility, and subepidermal split on hematoxylin-eosin staining, a diagnosis of DEB, pruriginosa subtype (DEB-P), was supported. Gabapentin provided partial relief, and addition of dupilumab resulted in significant symptomatic improvement. DEB results from various genetic variants encoding type 7 collagen, a major component of anchoring fibrils essential for adhesion along the dermo-epidermal junction. DEB-P is a rare subtype described in 1994, with a variety of genetic variants ofCOL7A1, including the specific variant present in this patient.1,2DEB-P is often autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive and sporadic cases have been reported.2Patients often lack blistering and instead show markedly pruritic papules commonly on lower legs. Pathology typically shows orthohyperkeratosis and acanthosis with perivascular mononuclear infiltration, in addition to a subepidermal separation as noted in this patient.1However, more brisk infiltrates, including eosinophils, have been observed.3Milia and fibrosis may also be present. Diagnosis is made with a combination of consistent clinical features, pathology, family history, genetic testing, and/or immunofluorescence mapping. In this patient, we initially considered lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and prurigo nodularis as differential diagnoses. Absence of dense lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar change, sawtooth rete ridges, and lack of colloid bodies opposed a diagnosis of lichen planus, as did the decades-long duration of her disease.4There was no significant amyloid deposition to support lichen amyloidosis.5The repeat biopsy showed a convincing subepidermal separation, which did not support simple prurigo nodularis. This separation is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita along with the sparse inflammatory infiltrate, but the direct immunofluorescence, serum examination, and lack of blistering clinically did not support this diagnosis.6The pauci-inflammatory infiltrate and subepidermal separation were consistent with epidermolysis bullosa, and genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis of DEB. In conjunction with the clinical findings, this patient's presentation is consistent with DEB-P. Although pruritus is a common symptom in all forms of epidermolysis bullosa, those with DEB-P have particularly severe itching.2This is associated with the distinctive clinical presentation: extensive scaling, papulonodules coalescing into plaques primarily found on lower legs, often with a linear configuration, resembling lichen amyloidosis or lichen planus, thus leading to diagnostic confusion.7The skin is mostly spared elsewhere. Intact blisters are rarely seen, but scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy can be present.3Onset may be at birth but can be delayed by several decades, adding to the potential for misdiagnosis.3,7 The basis for the intense pruritus is unclear, but dysregulation of cytokine pathways, particularly those related to Th1, Th2, and Th17, an impaired skin barrier, inflammation associated with wound healing, and abnormal epidermal sensory nerve activation have been implicated in the pathogenesis.2Treatment for the pruritus associated with DEB-P typically includes antihistamines, neuropathic agents, topical steroids, and adequate wound care, but these may not be sufficient. Cyclosporine and thalidomide have been used successfully.8There are several recent reports of dupilumab being highly effective, as with this patient, supporting a Th2-mediated process.9,10This case report highlights a rare form of DEB, which has a largely nonblistering, papulonodular presentation, making the diagnosis challenging, and reminds us that sometimes genetic diseases may not be diagnosed until adulthood.

dialogue_history.text: Based on the clinical presentation and biopsy results, the most appropriate next step in management is to consider the diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (option B). The patient's history of pruritic lesions, skin sloughing, and the histopathological findings of subepidermal separation align well with this condition. Additionally, the involvement of dystrophic toenails and the previous biopsies suggest a potential autoimmune mechanism, which is characteristic of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. While lichen amyloidosis and lichen planus could present with similar skin findings, the specific details favor an autoimmune blistering disorder like epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. Further diagnostic confirmation through the collagen type 7 antibody assay will provide additional clarity.

However, the intense pruritus, linear lichenoid papules, and lack of mucosal involvement are atypical for classic EBA. I'd emphasize that lichen planus pemphigoides or bullous lichen planus should also be high on the differential, as they can show similar immunofluorescence patterns and respond to different treatments.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is

  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Repeat hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed sparse perivascular to focally lichenoid dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis without vacuolar change or eosinophilic infiltration (Figure, B). Areas of acanthosis, orthohyperkeratosis, and epidermal thinning were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed no linear deposition of immunoreactants at the basement membrane zone, and the result of the type 7 collagen enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay was negative. Genetic testing identified heterozygosity in theCOL7A1gene for a sequence variant,c.7247G>T, confirming the diagnosis of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). In the setting of lichenified papules on the patient’s extremities, severe refractory pruritus, skin fragility, and subepidermal split on hematoxylin-eosin staining, a diagnosis of DEB, pruriginosa subtype (DEB-P), was supported. Gabapentin provided partial relief, and addition of dupilumab resulted in significant symptomatic improvement. DEB results from various genetic variants encoding type 7 collagen, a major component of anchoring fibrils essential for adhesion along the dermo-epidermal junction. DEB-P is a rare subtype described in 1994, with a variety of genetic variants ofCOL7A1, including the specific variant present in this patient.1,2DEB-P is often autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive and sporadic cases have been reported.2Patients often lack blistering and instead show markedly pruritic papules commonly on lower legs. Pathology typically shows orthohyperkeratosis and acanthosis with perivascular mononuclear infiltration, in addition to a subepidermal separation as noted in this patient.1However, more brisk infiltrates, including eosinophils, have been observed.3Milia and fibrosis may also be present. Diagnosis is made with a combination of consistent clinical features, pathology, family history, genetic testing, and/or immunofluorescence mapping. In this patient, we initially considered lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and prurigo nodularis as differential diagnoses. Absence of dense lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar change, sawtooth rete ridges, and lack of colloid bodies opposed a diagnosis of lichen planus, as did the decades-long duration of her disease.4There was no significant amyloid deposition to support lichen amyloidosis.5The repeat biopsy showed a convincing subepidermal separation, which did not support simple prurigo nodularis. This separation is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita along with the sparse inflammatory infiltrate, but the direct immunofluorescence, serum examination, and lack of blistering clinically did not support this diagnosis.6The pauci-inflammatory infiltrate and subepidermal separation were consistent with epidermolysis bullosa, and genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis of DEB. In conjunction with the clinical findings, this patient's presentation is consistent with DEB-P. Although pruritus is a common symptom in all forms of epidermolysis bullosa, those with DEB-P have particularly severe itching.2This is associated with the distinctive clinical presentation: extensive scaling, papulonodules coalescing into plaques primarily found on lower legs, often with a linear configuration, resembling lichen amyloidosis or lichen planus, thus leading to diagnostic confusion.7The skin is mostly spared elsewhere. Intact blisters are rarely seen, but scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy can be present.3Onset may be at birth but can be delayed by several decades, adding to the potential for misdiagnosis.3,7 The basis for the intense pruritus is unclear, but dysregulation of cytokine pathways, particularly those related to Th1, Th2, and Th17, an impaired skin barrier, inflammation associated with wound healing, and abnormal epidermal sensory nerve activation have been implicated in the pathogenesis.2Treatment for the pruritus associated with DEB-P typically includes antihistamines, neuropathic agents, topical steroids, and adequate wound care, but these may not be sufficient. Cyclosporine and thalidomide have been used successfully.8There are several recent reports of dupilumab being highly effective, as with this patient, supporting a Th2-mediated process.9,10This case report highlights a rare form of DEB, which has a largely nonblistering, papulonodular presentation, making the diagnosis challenging, and reminds us that sometimes genetic diseases may not be diagnosed until adulthood.

case_info.explanation: Repeat hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed sparse perivascular to focally lichenoid dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis without vacuolar change or eosinophilic infiltration (Figure, B). Areas of acanthosis, orthohyperkeratosis, and epidermal thinning were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed no linear deposition of immunoreactants at the basement membrane zone, and the result of the type 7 collagen enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay was negative. Genetic testing identified heterozygosity in theCOL7A1gene for a sequence variant,c.7247G>T, confirming the diagnosis of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). In the setting of lichenified papules on the patient’s extremities, severe refractory pruritus, skin fragility, and subepidermal split on hematoxylin-eosin staining, a diagnosis of DEB, pruriginosa subtype (DEB-P), was supported. Gabapentin provided partial relief, and addition of dupilumab resulted in significant symptomatic improvement. DEB results from various genetic variants encoding type 7 collagen, a major component of anchoring fibrils essential for adhesion along the dermo-epidermal junction. DEB-P is a rare subtype described in 1994, with a variety of genetic variants ofCOL7A1, including the specific variant present in this patient.1,2DEB-P is often autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive and sporadic cases have been reported.2Patients often lack blistering and instead show markedly pruritic papules commonly on lower legs. Pathology typically shows orthohyperkeratosis and acanthosis with perivascular mononuclear infiltration, in addition to a subepidermal separation as noted in this patient.1However, more brisk infiltrates, including eosinophils, have been observed.3Milia and fibrosis may also be present. Diagnosis is made with a combination of consistent clinical features, pathology, family history, genetic testing, and/or immunofluorescence mapping. In this patient, we initially considered lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and prurigo nodularis as differential diagnoses. Absence of dense lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar change, sawtooth rete ridges, and lack of colloid bodies opposed a diagnosis of lichen planus, as did the decades-long duration of her disease.4There was no significant amyloid deposition to support lichen amyloidosis.5The repeat biopsy showed a convincing subepidermal separation, which did not support simple prurigo nodularis. This separation is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita along with the sparse inflammatory infiltrate, but the direct immunofluorescence, serum examination, and lack of blistering clinically did not support this diagnosis.6The pauci-inflammatory infiltrate and subepidermal separation were consistent with epidermolysis bullosa, and genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis of DEB. In conjunction with the clinical findings, this patient's presentation is consistent with DEB-P. Although pruritus is a common symptom in all forms of epidermolysis bullosa, those with DEB-P have particularly severe itching.2This is associated with the distinctive clinical presentation: extensive scaling, papulonodules coalescing into plaques primarily found on lower legs, often with a linear configuration, resembling lichen amyloidosis or lichen planus, thus leading to diagnostic confusion.7The skin is mostly spared elsewhere. Intact blisters are rarely seen, but scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy can be present.3Onset may be at birth but can be delayed by several decades, adding to the potential for misdiagnosis.3,7 The basis for the intense pruritus is unclear, but dysregulation of cytokine pathways, particularly those related to Th1, Th2, and Th17, an impaired skin barrier, inflammation associated with wound healing, and abnormal epidermal sensory nerve activation have been implicated in the pathogenesis.2Treatment for the pruritus associated with DEB-P typically includes antihistamines, neuropathic agents, topical steroids, and adequate wound care, but these may not be sufficient. Cyclosporine and thalidomide have been used successfully.8There are several recent reports of dupilumab being highly effective, as with this patient, supporting a Th2-mediated process.9,10This case report highlights a rare form of DEB, which has a largely nonblistering, papulonodular presentation, making the diagnosis challenging, and reminds us that sometimes genetic diseases may not be diagnosed until adulthood.

case_info.explanation: Repeat hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed sparse perivascular to focally lichenoid dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis without vacuolar change or eosinophilic infiltration (Figure, B). Areas of acanthosis, orthohyperkeratosis, and epidermal thinning were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed no linear deposition of immunoreactants at the basement membrane zone, and the result of the type 7 collagen enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay was negative. Genetic testing identified heterozygosity in theCOL7A1gene for a sequence variant,c.7247G>T, confirming the diagnosis of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). In the setting of lichenified papules on the patient’s extremities, severe refractory pruritus, skin fragility, and subepidermal split on hematoxylin-eosin staining, a diagnosis of DEB, pruriginosa subtype (DEB-P), was supported. Gabapentin provided partial relief, and addition of dupilumab resulted in significant symptomatic improvement. DEB results from various genetic variants encoding type 7 collagen, a major component of anchoring fibrils essential for adhesion along the dermo-epidermal junction. DEB-P is a rare subtype described in 1994, with a variety of genetic variants ofCOL7A1, including the specific variant present in this patient.1,2DEB-P is often autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive and sporadic cases have been reported.2Patients often lack blistering and instead show markedly pruritic papules commonly on lower legs. Pathology typically shows orthohyperkeratosis and acanthosis with perivascular mononuclear infiltration, in addition to a subepidermal separation as noted in this patient.1However, more brisk infiltrates, including eosinophils, have been observed.3Milia and fibrosis may also be present. Diagnosis is made with a combination of consistent clinical features, pathology, family history, genetic testing, and/or immunofluorescence mapping. In this patient, we initially considered lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and prurigo nodularis as differential diagnoses. Absence of dense lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar change, sawtooth rete ridges, and lack of colloid bodies opposed a diagnosis of lichen planus, as did the decades-long duration of her disease.4There was no significant amyloid deposition to support lichen amyloidosis.5The repeat biopsy showed a convincing subepidermal separation, which did not support simple prurigo nodularis. This separation is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita along with the sparse inflammatory infiltrate, but the direct immunofluorescence, serum examination, and lack of blistering clinically did not support this diagnosis.6The pauci-inflammatory infiltrate and subepidermal separation were consistent with epidermolysis bullosa, and genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis of DEB. In conjunction with the clinical findings, this patient's presentation is consistent with DEB-P. Although pruritus is a common symptom in all forms of epidermolysis bullosa, those with DEB-P have particularly severe itching.2This is associated with the distinctive clinical presentation: extensive scaling, papulonodules coalescing into plaques primarily found on lower legs, often with a linear configuration, resembling lichen amyloidosis or lichen planus, thus leading to diagnostic confusion.7The skin is mostly spared elsewhere. Intact blisters are rarely seen, but scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy can be present.3Onset may be at birth but can be delayed by several decades, adding to the potential for misdiagnosis.3,7 The basis for the intense pruritus is unclear, but dysregulation of cytokine pathways, particularly those related to Th1, Th2, and Th17, an impaired skin barrier, inflammation associated with wound healing, and abnormal epidermal sensory nerve activation have been implicated in the pathogenesis.2Treatment for the pruritus associated with DEB-P typically includes antihistamines, neuropathic agents, topical steroids, and adequate wound care, but these may not be sufficient. You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her 40s presented to our immunobullous disease clinic with a 30-year history of an intensely pruritic eruption predominantly affecting her legs, forearms, and hands. She also reported a nearly lifelong tendency for skin sloughing with minimal trauma but denied mucosal or nail involvement. Her great toenails and 2 others were dystrophic, but all other nails appeared normal. No blisters were present, and the remaining examination results were otherwise unremarkable. A biopsy for direct immunofluorescence was taken; a repeat biopsy for hematoxylin-eosin staining was performed; and serum was obtained for collagen type 7 antibody assay and genetic testing to rule out epidermolysis bullosa.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:

    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are

imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.

  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 5.9. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, Hundreds of reddish-brown 2- to 5-mm flat-topped papules are scattered on the patient’s bilateral lower extremities and dorsal feet with great toenail dystrophy. case_info.explanation: Repeat hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed sparse perivascular to focally lichenoid dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis without vacuolar change or eosinophilic infiltration (Figure, B). Areas of acanthosis, orthohyperkeratosis, and epidermal thinning were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed no linear deposition of immunoreactants at the basement membrane zone, and the result of the type 7 collagen enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay was negative. Genetic testing identified heterozygosity in theCOL7A1gene for a sequence variant,c.7247G>T, confirming the diagnosis of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). In the setting of lichenified papules on the patient’s extremities, severe refractory pruritus, skin fragility, and subepidermal split on hematoxylin-eosin staining, a diagnosis of DEB, pruriginosa subtype (DEB-P), was supported. Gabapentin provided partial relief, and addition of dupilumab resulted in significant symptomatic improvement. DEB results from various genetic variants encoding type 7 collagen, a major component of anchoring fibrils essential for adhesion along the dermo-epidermal junction. DEB-P is a rare subtype described in 1994, with a variety of genetic variants ofCOL7A1, including the specific variant present in this patient.1,2DEB-P is often autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive and sporadic cases have been reported.2Patients often lack blistering and instead show markedly pruritic papules commonly on lower legs. Pathology typically shows orthohyperkeratosis and acanthosis with perivascular mononuclear infiltration, in addition to a subepidermal separation as noted in this patient.1However, more brisk infiltrates, including eosinophils, have been observed.3Milia and fibrosis may also be present. Diagnosis is made with a combination of consistent clinical features, pathology, family history, genetic testing, and/or immunofluorescence mapping. In this patient, we initially considered lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and prurigo nodularis as differential diagnoses. Absence of dense lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar change, sawtooth rete ridges, and lack of colloid bodies opposed a diagnosis of lichen planus, as did the decades-long duration of her disease.4There was no significant amyloid deposition to support lichen amyloidosis.5The repeat biopsy showed a convincing subepidermal separation, which did not support simple prurigo nodularis. This separation is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita along with the sparse inflammatory infiltrate, but the direct immunofluorescence, serum examination, and lack of blistering clinically did not support this diagnosis.6The pauci-inflammatory infiltrate and subepidermal separation were consistent with epidermolysis bullosa, and genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis of DEB. In conjunction with the clinical findings, this patient's presentation is consistent with DEB-P. Although pruritus is a common symptom in all forms of epidermolysis bullosa, those with DEB-P have particularly severe itching.2This is associated with the distinctive clinical presentation: extensive scaling, papulonodules coalescing into plaques primarily found on lower legs, often with a linear configuration, resembling lichen amyloidosis or lichen planus, thus leading to diagnostic confusion.7The skin is mostly spared elsewhere. Intact blisters are rarely seen, but scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy can be present.3Onset may be at birth but can be delayed by several decades, adding to the potential for misdiagnosis.3,7 The basis for the intense pruritus is unclear, but dysregulation of cytokine pathways, particularly those related to Th1, Th2, and Th17, an impaired skin barrier, inflammation associated with wound healing, and abnormal epidermal sensory nerve activation have been implicated in the pathogenesis.2Treatment for the pruritus associated with DEB-P typically includes antihistamines, neuropathic agents, topical steroids, and adequate wound care, but these may not be sufficient. Cyclosporine and thalidomide have been used successfully.8There are several recent reports of dupilumab being highly effective, as with this patient, supporting a Th2-mediated process.9,10This case report highlights a rare form of DEB, which has a largely nonblistering, papulonodular presentation, making the diagnosis challenging, and reminds us that sometimes genetic diseases may not be diagnosed until adulthood.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 40s presented to our immunobullous disease clinic with a 30-year history of an intensely pruritic eruption predominantly affecting her legs, forearms, and hands. She also reported a nearly lifelong tendency for skin sloughing with minimal trauma but denied mucosal or nail involvement. Previous treatments, including topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and oral antihistamines, had been ineffective. Her family history was unknown. Results of prior biopsies at an outside institution showed perivascular and focal lichenoid lymphohistiocytic inflammation with milia and a subepidermal separation, suggesting possible epidermolysis bullosa acquisita vs artifactual separation. Physical examination was notable for hundreds of brown to violaceous scaly, lichenoid papules on the anterior lower legs, dorsal feet (Figure, A) and dorsal forearms, some with a linear configuration, with a few scattered lesions on the upper and lower back. Her great toenails and 2 others were dystrophic, but all other nails appeared normal. No blisters were present, and the remaining examination results were otherwise unremarkable. A biopsy for direct immunofluorescence was taken; a repeat biopsy for hematoxylin-eosin staining was performed; and serum was obtained for collagen type 7 antibody assay and genetic testing to rule out epidermolysis bullosa.
case_info.caption: A, Hundreds of reddish-brown 2- to 5-mm flat-topped papules are scattered on the patient’s bilateral lower extremities and dorsal feet with great toenail dystrophy. B, Histopathological imaging shows basketweave hyperkeratosis overlying areas of acanthosis and epidermal thinning and sparse lymphohistiocytic perivascular dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: Repeat hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed sparse perivascular to focally lichenoid dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis without vacuolar change or eosinophilic infiltration (Figure, B). Areas of acanthosis, orthohyperkeratosis, and epidermal thinning were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed no linear deposition of immunoreactants at the basement membrane zone, and the result of the type 7 collagen enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay was negative. Genetic testing identified heterozygosity in theCOL7A1gene for a sequence variant,c.7247G>T, confirming the diagnosis of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). In the setting of lichenified papules on the patient’s extremities, severe refractory pruritus, skin fragility, and subepidermal split on hematoxylin-eosin staining, a diagnosis of DEB, pruriginosa subtype (DEB-P), was supported. Gabapentin provided partial relief, and addition of dupilumab resulted in significant symptomatic improvement. DEB results from various genetic variants encoding type 7 collagen, a major component of anchoring fibrils essential for adhesion along the dermo-epidermal junction. DEB-P is a rare subtype described in 1994, with a variety of genetic variants ofCOL7A1, including the specific variant present in this patient.1,2DEB-P is often autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive and sporadic cases have been reported.2Patients often lack blistering and instead show markedly pruritic papules commonly on lower legs. Pathology typically shows orthohyperkeratosis and acanthosis with perivascular mononuclear infiltration, in addition to a subepidermal separation as noted in this patient.1However, more brisk infiltrates, including eosinophils, have been observed.3Milia and fibrosis may also be present. Diagnosis is made with a combination of consistent clinical features, pathology, family history, genetic testing, and/or immunofluorescence mapping. In this patient, we initially considered lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and prurigo nodularis as differential diagnoses. Absence of dense lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar change, sawtooth rete ridges, and lack of colloid bodies opposed a diagnosis of lichen planus, as did the decades-long duration of her disease.4There was no significant amyloid deposition to support lichen amyloidosis.5The repeat biopsy showed a convincing subepidermal separation, which did not support simple prurigo nodularis. This separation is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita along with the sparse inflammatory infiltrate, but the direct immunofluorescence, serum examination, and lack of blistering clinically did not support this diagnosis.6The pauci-inflammatory infiltrate and subepidermal separation were consistent with epidermolysis bullosa, and genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis of DEB. In conjunction with the clinical findings, this patient's presentation is consistent with DEB-P. Although pruritus is a common symptom in all forms of epidermolysis bullosa, those with DEB-P have particularly severe itching.2This is associated with the distinctive clinical presentation: extensive scaling, papulonodules coalescing into plaques primarily found on lower legs, often with a linear configuration, resembling lichen amyloidosis or lichen planus, thus leading to diagnostic confusion.7The skin is mostly spared elsewhere. Intact blisters are rarely seen, but scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy can be present.3Onset may be at birth but can be delayed by several decades, adding to the potential for misdiagnosis.3,7 The basis for the intense pruritus is unclear, but dysregulation of cytokine pathways, particularly those related to Th1, Th2, and Th17, an impaired skin barrier, inflammation associated with wound healing, and abnormal epidermal sensory nerve activation have been implicated in the pathogenesis.2Treatment for the pruritus associated with DEB-P typically includes antihistamines, neuropathic agents, topical steroids, and adequate wound care, but these may not be sufficient. Cyclosporine and thalidomide have been used successfully.8There are several recent reports of dupilumab being highly effective, as with this patient, supporting a Th2-mediated process.9,10This case report highlights a rare form of DEB, which has a largely nonblistering, papulonodular presentation, making the diagnosis challenging, and reminds us that sometimes genetic diseases may not be diagnosed until adulthood.

case_info.explanation: Repeat hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed sparse perivascular to focally lichenoid dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis without vacuolar change or eosinophilic infiltration (Figure, B). Areas of acanthosis, orthohyperkeratosis, and epidermal thinning were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed no linear deposition of immunoreactants at the basement membrane zone, and the result of the type 7 collagen enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay was negative. Genetic testing identified heterozygosity in theCOL7A1gene for a sequence variant,c.7247G>T, confirming the diagnosis of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). In the setting of lichenified papules on the patient’s extremities, severe refractory pruritus, skin fragility, and subepidermal split on hematoxylin-eosin staining, a diagnosis of DEB, pruriginosa subtype (DEB-P), was supported. Gabapentin provided partial relief, and addition of dupilumab resulted in significant symptomatic improvement. DEB results from various genetic variants encoding type 7 collagen, a major component of anchoring fibrils essential for adhesion along the dermo-epidermal junction. DEB-P is a rare subtype described in 1994, with a variety of genetic variants ofCOL7A1, including the specific variant present in this patient.1,2DEB-P is often autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive and sporadic cases have been reported.2Patients often lack blistering and instead show markedly pruritic papules commonly on lower legs. Pathology typically shows orthohyperkeratosis and acanthosis with perivascular mononuclear infiltration, in addition to a subepidermal separation as noted in this patient.1However, more brisk infiltrates, including eosinophils, have been observed.3Milia and fibrosis may also be present. Diagnosis is made with a combination of consistent clinical features, pathology, family history, genetic testing, and/or immunofluorescence mapping. In this patient, we initially considered lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and prurigo nodularis as differential diagnoses. Absence of dense lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar change, sawtooth rete ridges, and lack of colloid bodies opposed a diagnosis of lichen planus, as did the decades-long duration of her disease.4There was no significant amyloid deposition to support lichen amyloidosis.5The repeat biopsy showed a convincing subepidermal separation, which did not support simple prurigo nodularis. This separation is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita along with the sparse inflammatory infiltrate, but the direct immunofluorescence, serum examination, and lack of blistering clinically did not support this diagnosis.6The pauci-inflammatory infiltrate and subepidermal separation were consistent with epidermolysis bullosa, and genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis of DEB. In conjunction with the clinical findings, this patient's presentation is consistent with DEB-P. Although pruritus is a common symptom in all forms of epidermolysis bullosa, those with DEB-P have particularly severe itching.2This is associated with the distinctive clinical presentation: extensive scaling, papulonodules coalescing into plaques primarily found on lower legs, often with a linear configuration, resembling lichen amyloidosis or lichen planus, thus leading to diagnostic confusion.7The skin is mostly spared elsewhere. Intact blisters are rarely seen, but scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy can be present.3Onset may be at birth but can be delayed by several decades, adding to the potential for misdiagnosis.3,7 The basis for the intense pruritus is unclear, but dysregulation of cytokine pathways, particularly those related to Th1, Th2, and Th17, an impaired skin barrier, inflammation associated with wound healing, and abnormal epidermal sensory nerve activation have been implicated in the pathogenesis.2Treatment for the pruritus associated with DEB-P typically includes antihistamines, neuropathic agents, topical steroids, and adequate wound care, but these may not be sufficient. Cyclosporine and thalidomide have been used successfully.8There are several recent reports of dupilumab being highly effective, as with this patient, supporting a Th2-mediated process.9,10This case report highlights a rare form of DEB, which has a largely nonblistering, papulonodular presentation, making the diagnosis challenging, and reminds us that sometimes genetic diseases may not be diagnosed until adulthood.

case_info.explanation: Repeat hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed sparse perivascular to focally lichenoid dermatitis with subepidermal separation and dermal fibrosis without vacuolar change or eosinophilic infiltration (Figure, B). Areas of acanthosis, orthohyperkeratosis, and epidermal thinning were present. Direct immunofluorescence showed no linear deposition of immunoreactants at the basement membrane zone, and the result of the type 7 collagen enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay was negative. Genetic testing identified heterozygosity in theCOL7A1gene for a sequence variant,c.7247G>T, confirming the diagnosis of dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). In the setting of lichenified papules on the patient’s extremities, severe refractory pruritus, skin fragility, and subepidermal split on hematoxylin-eosin staining, a diagnosis of DEB, pruriginosa subtype (DEB-P), was supported. Gabapentin provided partial relief, and addition of dupilumab resulted in significant symptomatic improvement. DEB results from various genetic variants encoding type 7 collagen, a major component of anchoring fibrils essential for adhesion along the dermo-epidermal junction. DEB-P is a rare subtype described in 1994, with a variety of genetic variants ofCOL7A1, including the specific variant present in this patient.1,2DEB-P is often autosomal dominant, but autosomal recessive and sporadic cases have been reported.2Patients often lack blistering and instead show markedly pruritic papules commonly on lower legs. Pathology typically shows orthohyperkeratosis and acanthosis with perivascular mononuclear infiltration, in addition to a subepidermal separation as noted in this patient.1However, more brisk infiltrates, including eosinophils, have been observed.3Milia and fibrosis may also be present. Diagnosis is made with a combination of consistent clinical features, pathology, family history, genetic testing, and/or immunofluorescence mapping. In this patient, we initially considered lichen planus, lichen amyloidosis, and prurigo nodularis as differential diagnoses. Absence of dense lichenoid inflammation, vacuolar change, sawtooth rete ridges, and lack of colloid bodies opposed a diagnosis of lichen planus, as did the decades-long duration of her disease.4There was no significant amyloid deposition to support lichen amyloidosis.5The repeat biopsy showed a convincing subepidermal separation, which did not support simple prurigo nodularis. This separation is seen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita along with the sparse inflammatory infiltrate, but the direct immunofluorescence, serum examination, and lack of blistering clinically did not support this diagnosis.6The pauci-inflammatory infiltrate and subepidermal separation were consistent with epidermolysis bullosa, and genetic testing confirmed a diagnosis of DEB. In conjunction with the clinical findings, this patient's presentation is consistent with DEB-P. Although pruritus is a common symptom in all forms of epidermolysis bullosa, those with DEB-P have particularly severe itching.2This is associated with the distinctive clinical presentation: extensive scaling, papulonodules coalescing into plaques primarily found on lower legs, often with a linear configuration, resembling lichen amyloidosis or lichen planus, thus leading to diagnostic confusion.7The skin is mostly spared elsewhere. Intact blisters are rarely seen, but scarring, milia, and nail dystrophy can be present.3Onset may be at birth but can be delayed by several decades, adding to the potential for misdiagnosis.3,7 The basis for the intense pruritus is unclear, but dysregulation of cytokine pathways, particularly those related to Th1, Th2, and Th17, an impaired skin barrier, inflammation associated with wound healing, and abnormal epidermal sensory nerve activation have been implicated in the pathogenesis.2Treatment for the pruritus associated with DEB-P typically includes antihistamines, neuropathic agents, topical steroids, and adequate wound care, but these may not be sufficient. Cyclosporine and thalidomide have been used successfully.8There are several recent reports of dupilumab being highly effective, as with this patient, supporting a Th2-mediated process.9,10This case report highlights a rare form of DEB, which has a largely nonblistering, papulonodular presentation, making the diagnosis challenging, and reminds us that sometimes genetic diseases may not be diagnosed until adulthood.

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her 40s presented to our immunobullous disease clinic with a 30-year history of an intensely pruritic eruption predominantly affecting her legs, forearms, and hands. She also reported a nearly lifelong tendency for skin sloughing with minimal trauma but denied mucosal or nail involvement. Previous treatments, including topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and oral antihistamines, had been ineffective. Her family history was unknown. Results of prior biopsies at an outside institution showed perivascular and focal lichenoid lymphohistiocytic inflammation with milia and a subepidermal separation, suggesting possible epidermolysis bullosa acquisita vs artifactual separation. Physical examination was notable for hundreds of brown to violaceous scaly, lichenoid papules on the anterior lower legs, dorsal feet (Figure, A) and dorsal forearms, some with a linear configuration, with a few scattered lesions on the upper and lower back. Her great toenails and 2 others were dystrophic, but all other nails appeared normal. No blisters were present, and the remaining examination results were otherwise unremarkable. A biopsy for direct immunofluorescence was taken; a repeat biopsy for hematoxylin-eosin staining was performed; and serum was obtained for collagen type 7 antibody assay and genetic testing to rule out epidermolysis bullosa.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

}
